text: It's tempting to think of Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot capacity as small, medium, and large discounts on one sliding scale. They're not. Each one trades a different kind of flexibility for a different kind of discount, and picking the wrong one for a workload doesn't just leave savings on the table — it can leave you paying for capacity you can't use.

A Reserved Instance or Azure Reservation is a one- or three-year commitment to a specific instance type and region, in exchange for a lower rate — the capacity itself behaves exactly like on-demand, with zero interruption risk. A Savings Plan commits to a dollar-per-hour of compute spend instead, applying that discount automatically across whatever eligible instance types you're actually running. Spot capacity sells unused data center capacity at the deepest discount of the three, but the provider can reclaim it with as little as about two minutes' notice.

That tradeoff decides where each one belongs. Reserved capacity fits the steady-state baseline that isn't going to change shape. A Savings Plan fits compute that's steady in aggregate but shifts shape — different instance families, autoscaled fleets, an organization still actively right-sizing. Spot fits only workloads that are genuinely fault-tolerant: stateless batch jobs that checkpoint and resume, queue-backed worker pools, CI/CD build agents. It is never a fit for a stateful database primary or a single-instance service with no redundancy, where a two-minute eviction notice would mean a real outage.

A mature cost strategy blends all three, in a specific order. Right-size first, because committing to a discount on an oversized instance just locks in the waste for the length of the term. Put Reserved Instances on the stable baseline, Savings Plans on the compute that shifts shape, and layer Spot on top as additional capacity for workloads explicitly built to tolerate interruption — never as the only capacity behind anything that has to stay up.

Get that order backwards — committing before right-sizing, or putting a stateful service on Spot because the discount looked good — and a cost optimization effort turns into a reliability incident. Next up: autoscaling, which belongs in this same toolkit as a deliberate cost lever, not just a performance one.
